newsitem.title: INDIA: Notorious criminal says will soon leave prison.
newsitem.headline: Notorious criminal says will soon leave prison.

text.p: Charles Sobhraj, whose criminal exploits across Asia were the subject of two books, won bail on Thursday and said he would soon leave the maximum security Indian prison where he has been held for more than 20 years.
Chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar granted Sobhraj bail in an extradition case and ordered him to furnish surety of 30,000 rupees ($835) and personal bonds of the same amount.
Sobhraj, 52, told reporters in a crowded New Delhi courtroom that one of his two sisters or his brother-in-law would pledge the surety in a day or two.
"It feels great," said Sobhraj, wearing a blue cap and flanked by three policemen but without handcuffs.

Sobhraj, a French citizen born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother, was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. Then a gaunt, good-looking 26-year-old, he jumped bail before his trial could be held.
India convicted Sobhraj in 1978 of murdering a French tourist. He was acquitted 20 months later on appeal, but remained in New Delhi's notorious Tihar jail on lesser charges.
Another judge sentenced Sobhraj to life imprisonment in 1982 for poisoning an Israeli tourist to death, but again he was acquitted on appeal.
In 1986, Sobhraj escaped while being held pending an extradition request from Thailand to face charges of murder and attempted murder. He was recaptured 24 days later.
Thailand's 20-year statute of limitations later expired and Thai police said late last year that Sobhraj no longer could be tried on their charges.

In Bangkok, Major General Watcharapol Prasarnrajkit, chief of the Thai Interpol police, told Reuters on Thursday: "We have already informed our Indian counterparts that Thailand does not want him to be extradited here any more.
"All the related cases against him have also expired because the warrant against him was issued in May 1976."
But in Hong Kong, police said on Thursday that they still wanted to interview Sobhraj about drugging and robbery cases in the British colony in the 1970s.

Assistant Commissioner (Crime) Mike Horner said Hong Kong police had asked Interpol agents in India to clarify Sobhraj's legal status, including whether he had been released and whether he could leave the country.
"We have already asked New Delhi," said Horner. "We would certainly be interested in interviewing him if he was ever to set foot in Hong Kong."

Last Friday, an Indian judge granted Sobhraj bail in a case relating to his 1986 jail break. But his release was held up because the government had not told prison authorities that the Thai extradition warrant had lapsed.
Sobhraj's lawyer, Rajan Bakshi, told Reuters he would ask the Delhi High Court in a few days to cancel the Thai warrant.

Bakshi also said a hearing was set for April 30 in the jail-break case, but Sobhraj would not spend more time in jail even if convicted since the maximum penalty would be less than the 11 years he had served since his escape.
On Wednesday, Sobhraj said he would do social work and could work on a $15-million movie based on his life.
"I've adopted Buddhism," he said on Thursday. "First I'll go to temple and then to church."
Sobhraj said he would like to be released in the morning so he could go to the French Embassy to collect an identity card, without which he said Indian police could arrest him again.
"I think I will stay for a few months in India before going to France," he said, adding that his movements would not be restricted. But, "I have to watch my step carefully."
